meta.title: The Green That Gets Punctured
meta.skill_frame: Process: see why a repair must come after the damage.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.35, 5.59 and 5.98 on the three parts (104, 104 and 104 words), 5.56 together, near the band's floor. The load is a repair that follows the harm and must repeat: the mower seals the surface every week, and the holes only make sense after that damage is present.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for process 4.1, band 4.1, sequence 4. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A golf green pressed by its mower, then opened with hollow tines and sand, built so the repair comes after the damage and must repeat.
source.avoided: No course name, grass species, hole depth, or tournament. No claim about how often a green is opened beyond the passage.

session.difficulty_basis: The repair must follow the damage and repeats, so the order follows the harm rather than the task list.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: At dawn the mower crosses the green, cutting the grass to the same height in straight passes. The mower is heavy, and its wheels and roller press the soil under the blades. The mower deck is wide, so fewer passes cross the same ground. By the end of the week the surface is firm and smooth, which is what the players want. The same pressure closes the small spaces in the soil where air and water used to travel down to the roots. The green sits on a layer of sand and gravel, built to drain, and it drained well when it was new.
passage.part_2: Water now sits on the surface and runs toward the edge instead of sinking in. The crew tried watering longer, but the extra water ran off the same way, and the grass stayed shallow-rooted. Then they changed the work. A machine pushed hollow tines into the green and pulled out thin plugs of soil. Sand was swept into the open holes. Water entered the holes, and the roots followed it down. Within a week the surface felt softer underfoot and the ball stopped running so far. The plugs were carried off in a barrow and spread on the rough ground behind the shed.
passage.part_3: The puncturing comes after the mowing and after the watering, because it reopens what the mower pressed shut. Run it first, and the same wheels would close the holes within a day. The work is a repair, not a guard against harm. The mower keeps pressing the surface each week, so the holes are opened again every few weeks. The crew marks each pass on a chart and watches the calendar. A green that is opened on time stays soft underfoot all season. A chart on the shed wall lists the dates, and the crew checks it before the first mow of the month.

items.prompt: What presses the soil under the blades?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The mower's wheels and roller.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The second sentence says the mower is heavy and its wheels and roller press the soil under the blades.
tutor_only.tell: The mower is heavy. Its wheels and roller press the soil under the blades.
help: The second sentence names what presses the soil.
There are two parts to it.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.ask: Players matter later in the week. What presses the soil during mowing?

items.prompt: What happens to the small spaces in the soil under that pressure?

tutor_only.tell: The pressure closes the small spaces. Air and water can no longer travel down to the roots.
help: The fourth sentence says what the pressure does.

tutor_only.core_idea: They close, so air and water cannot travel down to the roots.
accept_ideas: air and water can no longer get down
